title: GRAM approximates multiple data-filtered models in a single run (Simple Stories)
statement: On Simple Stories, a single GRAM-trained model with module ablation closely matches separately data-filtered models across five capability profiles: retained capabilities stay near baseline (GRAM 0.95 vs filtering 0.96 aggregated compute ratio; e.g., Aliens retained 0.99 each), forgotten categories drop well below (e.g., 0.61 GRAM vs 0.65 filtering), and core performance stays near baseline (GRAM 0.94, filtering 0.96).
test_plan: Train an 8-layer 26M-parameter Transformer on Simple Stories (2M stories, 48 categories; 4 auxiliary categories chosen alphabetically, 44 core) for one epoch (batch 128, seq len 256). Implement GRAM with core MLP d=1856, auxiliary modules d=192, paf=1.0, pas=0.3, pcr=0.5; train data-filtered models on D1 ∪ Di per category and a full-data baseline. Fit power-law learning curves to baseline validation loss, compute compute ratios for each profile with module ablation, over 3 seeds.
evidence_in_paper: Figure 2 and Section 4: GRAM retain CR 0.95 vs filtering 0.96; core 0.94 vs 0.96; example forget values 0.61 vs 0.65.
success_criterion: Across the five profiles, GRAM's mean retain compute ratio is within ~0.02 of data filtering's (≈0.95 vs 0.96), forget compute ratios are well below retain (≈0.6 vs ≈0.95), and core compute ratio ≥0.9.

title: GRAM isolates realistic dual-use capabilities and matches data filtering at 800M scale
statement: An 800M-parameter GRAM model trained on web/code/arXiv core plus virology, cybersecurity, nuclear physics, and Lisp auxiliary domains matches data filtering and FT-LoRA on core, retain, and forget compute ratios (core ≈0.96, retain ≈0.97, forget ≈0.53, elicit ≈0.58 for GRAM vs filtering 0.99/0.96/0.53/0.54), while using baseline training FLOPS (vs 5× for filtering) and at most 1.1× active MLP parameters.
test_plan: Train 800M Transformers for one epoch on 16B core tokens (FineWeb-Edu, arXiv, The Stack minus Lisp) + 160M auxiliary tokens (~40M per domain). GRAM: core MLP d=6400, four aux modules d=640, pas=0.5, pcr=0.2, paf=4.0 (code)/3.0 (others). Baselines: all-data baseline, per-profile filtering, FT-LoRA, FT-Full, MaxEnt unlearning. Compute compute ratios via baseline learning curves; elicited forget via finetuning on 512 sequences per forget category, 3 seeds.
evidence_in_paper: Figure 4 and Section 5: per-method compute ratios and cost table (Filtering 5× FLOPS/5× total params; GRAM 1× FLOPS, 1.4× total params).
success_criterion: GRAM's core, retain, and forget compute ratios each fall within the 90% CI overlap of data filtering's values (core ≈0.96, retain ≈0.97, forget ≈0.53), and GRAM's elicited-forget compute ratio (≈0.58) is far below MaxEnt's (≈0.91).

title: Capability isolation improves with scale and GRAM tracks data filtering from 50M to 5B
statement: Across Chinchilla-optimal models from 50M to 5B parameters, data filtering's suppression of the forget capability widens with scale (forget compute ratio decreases) and elicited forget approaches forget, while GRAM and FT-LoRA closely track the data-filtered model's core, retain, forget, and elicited-forget compute ratios at every scale (with an anomalous GRAM retain gain at 5B attributed to hyperparameters).
test_plan: Train models at 50M, 100M, 200M, 400M, 800M, 2B, 5B parameters with Chinchilla-optimal token counts, auxiliary data at 1% of core, modules/adapters at 10% of MLP parameters. Compare baseline, GRAM, FT-LoRA, and Core+Virology data filtering. Compute core/retain(virology)/forget/elicited-forget compute ratios at each scale (3 seeds below 2B). Verify monotone decreasing forget trend with scale for filtering and that GRAM/FT-LoRA values lie within CIs of filtering at each scale.
evidence_in_paper: Figure 7 and Section 6: compute ratio vs model size for all four metrics; filtering forget decreases with scale; GRAM and FT-LoRA track filtering.
success_criterion: Forget compute ratio for filtering decreases as model size increases from 50M to 5B, and at each scale GRAM's core, retain, forget, and elicited-forget compute ratios match filtering's within the reported 90% CIs (excluding the noted 5B retain anomaly).

title: GRAM composes arbitrary capability subsets without degradation, unlike FT-LoRA
statement: Enabling multiple GRAM auxiliary modules at inference does not degrade retained-capability performance, supporting arbitrary capability subsets (2^(N-1) profiles) from one training run, whereas FT-LoRA degrades when more than one LoRA adapter is summed; GRAM achieves this despite never training with all modules active.
test_plan: Using the 800M dual-use models from C2, evaluate compute ratios in two configurations: (a) only the virology module/adapter active, (b) all four auxiliary modules/adapters active. Compare per-domain compute ratios for GRAM vs FT-LoRA across 3 seeds.
evidence_in_paper: Figure 5 and Section 5: GRAM retains high virology compute ratio in both configurations; FT-LoRA compute ratios drop across categories when all adapters are active.
success_criterion: GRAM's virology (retained) compute ratio with all modules active is statistically indistinguishable from the virology-only configuration, while FT-LoRA's compute ratios are lower in the all-adapters configuration.

title: GRAM outperforms filtering and FT-LoRA on capability removal under partial labeling
statement: With only 50% of training data labeled (unlabeled batches activate all modules for GRAM; unlabeled data treated as core for filtering/FT-LoRA), GRAM achieves a forget compute ratio of 0.60 ± 0.01 versus 0.85 ± 0.01 for both filtering and FT-LoRA, while maintaining competitive core performance (0.96 vs 0.99).
test_plan: Repeat the 800M dual-use training with labels randomly dropped for 50% of examples. GRAM: unlabeled batches run forward/backward through core and all auxiliary modules. Filtering/FT-LoRA: unlabeled data assigned to core. Measure core, forget, and elicited-forget compute ratios over 3 seeds.
evidence_in_paper: Figure 6 and Section 5: GRAM forget 0.60±0.01 vs 0.85±0.01 for filtering and FT-LoRA; core 0.96/0.99/0.99; elicit 0.76/0.85/0.86.
success_criterion: GRAM's aggregate forget compute ratio is significantly below filtering's and FT-LoRA's (≈0.60 vs ≈0.85, non-overlapping 90% CIs), with core compute ratio ≥0.95.

title: GRAM's training cost is independent of the number of capability profiles, yielding 5× savings over filtering
statement: GRAM produces all capability profiles in a single training run at baseline compute, whereas data filtering requires one run per profile; in the 5-profile setting this yields a 5× reduction in training FLOPS, with GRAM adding only ~1.4× total MLP parameters and ≤1.1× active parameters at inference.
test_plan: Compute FLOPS analytically (or via profiler) for the 800M setup: count training FLOPS for one GRAM run vs five filtering runs over matched token budgets, and count active/total MLP parameters per served profile. Verify GRAM's per-run token count equals the baseline's (auxiliary oversampling offset by core undersampling).
evidence_in_paper: Figure 4 right table: Filtering 5× train FLOPS, 5× total MLP params; GRAM 1× train FLOPS, 1× or 1.1× active, 1.4× total MLP params.
success_criterion: Measured/calculated GRAM training FLOPS equal baseline FLOPS (within 5%), filtering costs 5× baseline for 5 profiles, and GRAM active parameters per profile ≤1.1× baseline MLP.
